source_title: Can Indian employees sue companies over layoffs without notice? - India Today
source_excerpt:
Technology employees have reported abrupt layoffs through emails, HR meetings and access withdrawal. Indian law may require notice, compensation and due process depending on employment status.
Can a company fire you without notice, and can you sue if it does? The question has gained urgency as employees across the technology sector describe losing their jobs through sudden termination emails, unexpected HR meetings and the withdrawal of access to workplace systems.
The latest example comes from Innodata , where employees who said they were affected by layoffs described how they were informed that their roles had become redundant, lost access to work systems and received termination letters later.
On Reddit, a user identifying themselves as a process analyst said employees were called into a suddenly scheduled HR meeting and told their positions were being eliminated because a major client had reduced its volume of work.
The user alleged that employees were muted during the meeting, lost access to Microsoft Office applications within an hour and received termination letters on their personal email accounts later that day. Another user identifying themselves as an AI analyst said job cuts were taking place across India, the US and the Philippines as part of a project.
The pattern is not limited to Innodata. Oracle employees have also reported receiving early-morning termination emails, with some saying their access to workplace systems was withdrawn around the time they were informed their roles had been eliminated.
Amazon, meanwhile, cut up to 250 jobs in its devices and services unit on October 28, with employees notified by text messages and emails early that morning, reported news agency Reuters.
These developments highlight how quickly employees can find themselves out of a job, sometimes with little time to prepare for the financial and professional consequences. The Reddit accounts relating to Innodata have not been independently verified, and the circumstances of individual terminations can differ.
But they raise an important question for employees facing sudden job cuts: does a company have the right to terminate employment immediately, and what legal remedies are available if it fails to provide the notice, pay or compensation required under the applicable law or employment contract?
Legal experts say companies can restructure operations and reduce their workforce for genuine business reasons, but that does not automatically exempt them from their legal and contractual obligations.
“Indian law recognises an employer's right to reorganise its operations, rationalise costs and reduce its workforce in response to genuine commercial requirements. However, the existence of a legitimate business reason does not confer an unrestricted right to terminate employment without complying with applicable legal and contractual obligations,” said Akanksha Dua, Partner at Obhan Mason. CAN A COMPANY FIRE YOU WITHOUT NOTICE?
A company may have a genuine business reason to cut jobs, but that does not automatically mean it can disregard notice periods or other employment obligations. Whether an employee can be terminated with immediate effect depends on the employment contract, the employee’s actual duties, length of service and the labour laws applicable to the case.
An employer may be able to terminate employment immediately by paying salary in lieu of notice where the contract and applicable law permit it. For eligible workers covered by the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, retrenchment may also trigger statutory requirements relating to notice, compensation and procedure.
“A reduction in business assignments may constitute a legitimate commercial justification for restructuring, but it cannot independently override statutory and contractual employee protections,” Dua said.
Under the Code, qualifying workers who have completed one year of continuous service are generally entitled to written notice or wages in lieu of notice, along with retrenchment compensation calculated at 15 days’ average pay for every completed year of continuous service or part exceeding six months, subject to the applicable conditions. Certain establishments may face additional requirements, including a longer notice period and prior government permission.
These protections do not apply identically to every employee. People employed mainly in managerial or administrative roles may fall outside the Code’s definition of a worker and may have to rely more heavily on their contracts and other applicable laws.
Designation alone is not conclusive. The actual nature of an employee’s duties and responsibilities also matters. DOES LOSING ACCESS BEFORE A TERMINATION EMAIL MATTER?
DOES LOSING ACCESS BEFORE A TERMINATION EMAIL MATTER?
For employees who suddenly find themselves locked out of their work accounts, the timing of the formal termination letter may be important.
Ankit Rajgarhia, Partner at Bahuguna Law Associates, said the legal assessment should focus on the fact of termination rather than merely the form in which it is communicated.
“The test is the fact of termination rather than the form of the letter,” Rajgarhia said.
He said an access cut-off followed by a termination letter may give rise to an argument that the employment effectively ended on the earlier date. That date can matter when determining applicable notice and compensation obligations and when legal timelines begin.
However, disabling a laptop, email account or HR portal does not, by itself, establish that a termination is unlawful. The circumstances and the employer’s compliance with its legal and contractual obligations remain central to the assessment.
Dua similarly said that the removal of access or communication through email does not, on its own, determine whether a termination is illegal.
“The decisive issue is whether the employer has fulfilled the substantive and procedural obligations imposed by law and the employment relationship,” she said. CAN EMPLOYEES SUE FOR UNLAWFUL TERMINATION?
CAN EMPLOYEES SUE FOR UNLAWFUL TERMINATION?
Employees who believe they were terminated without legally required notice, pay or other benefits may be able to challenge the decision. The available remedy depends on their employment status and the nature of the dispute.
Eligible workers may pursue the statutory industrial dispute resolution process, including conciliation and adjudication before the competent Industrial Tribunal. Depending on the circumstances, relief may include recovery of statutory dues, compensation or, in appropriate cases, reinstatement.
Employees who do not qualify as workers under the relevant law may generally have to pursue contractual remedies. These can include claims for unpaid notice salary, outstanding remuneration and damages for breach of employment terms before the appropriate civil forum.
“An employee who is terminated without receiving legally mandated notice, salary in lieu of notice or other applicable employment benefits may challenge the termination through the appropriate legal forum,” Dua said.
The fact that an employee received a termination email or lost access to company systems does not automatically make the termination unlawful. Equally, citing a reduction in business or describing a role as redundant does not, by itself, establish that the employer has met every legal requirement. WHAT SHOULD EMPLOYEES DO AFTER A SUDDEN TERMINATION?
WHAT SHOULD EMPLOYEES DO AFTER A SUDDEN TERMINATION?
Employees who lose access to company systems should preserve employment documents and records they are lawfully able to retain. These may include appointment letters, employment contracts, payslips, salary-credit records, termination emails, messages about restructuring and evidence of when access was withdrawn.
They should check their notice-period clause, outstanding salary, leave encashment and other applicable separation benefits. If they believe the employer has failed to meet its obligations, they can seek advice from an employment lawyer or approach the relevant labour authority or legal forum, depending on their role and the nature of the claim.
Rajgarhia said the date of termination can be important because it may determine when statutory obligations and legal timelines begin. Employees should therefore retain the termination communication and its delivery record, alongside any messages explaining the reason for the job cut.
For employees outside worker-specific retrenchment protections, the employment contract may be particularly important in assessing their rights. Claims for unpaid dues may also need to be pursued through a different route from a challenge to the termination itself.
The key question is not simply whether a company can cut jobs in response to changing business conditions. It is whether it has followed the legal and contractual requirements that apply to each employee. - Ends
